section.heading: Certain hearings must be held in private

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding that relates to an intelligence and security decision, other than an exempt security record decision.
This section applies subject to:
section 149 (persons entitled to be present at hearings); and
section 158 (security certificates—responsible Minister).
Hearings to be held in private
The hearing of the proceeding must be held in private.
The Tribunal may, by order, give directions in relation to the persons who may be present at the hearing.

section.heading: Persons entitled to be present at hearings

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies:
in relation to a proceeding for review of an intelligence and security decision; and
subject to section 158 (security certificates—responsible Minister).
Persons entitled to be present
The applicant, and the applicant’s representative, are entitled to be present at the hearing of the proceeding when the Tribunal hears submissions made, or evidence adduced by:
the agency head (or representative); or
a relevant body.
The following are entitled to be present at the hearing of the proceeding when the Tribunal hears submissions made, or evidence adduced by the applicant (or representative):
the agency head (or representative);
a relevant body.

section.heading: Relevant bodies may adduce evidence and make submissions

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding for review of an intelligence and security decision.
Relevant bodies may adduce evidence and make submissions
A relevant body:
is entitled to adduce evidence and make submissions in the proceeding; and
for the purposes of the following sections, is taken to be a party to the proceeding:
section 56 (parties and their representatives to assist Tribunal);
section 66 (representation before Tribunal);
section 79 (Tribunal may give directions in relation to procedure for a proceeding);
section 151 (order of evidence and submissions);
section 152 (opportunity for further evidence and submissions).
When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding for review of an intelligence and security decision.
Order of presentation
Unless it determines otherwise, the Tribunal must hear initial evidence and submissions from the parties to the proceeding in the following order:
first—evidence adduced and submissions made by the agency head;
second—evidence adduced and submissions made by relevant bodies;
third—evidence adduced and submissions made by the applicant.

section.heading: Opportunity for further evidence and submissions

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding for review of an intelligence and security decision.
Further evidence and submissions
The Tribunal must give a party to the proceeding an opportunity to adduce further evidence and make further submissions in relation to the further evidence if:
the party presents the party’s case to the Tribunal; and
after that case is presented, another party adduces evidence; and
the Tribunal considers that, because of evidence adduced by the other party, the first-mentioned party should be further heard.

To avoid doubt, the Tribunal must not give the applicant particulars of evidence or a submission in contravention of another provision of this Act that prohibits or restricts the disclosure of those particulars.

section.heading: Tribunal may invite person to give evidence

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding in the Intelligence and Security jurisdictional area.
Tribunal may invite person to give evidence
The Tribunal may, on its own initiative and at any stage of the proceeding, invite a person to give evidence.
When this section applies
This section applies in relation to an intelligence and security decision, other than an exempt security record decision.
Dispute resolution
Subdivision C of Division 6 of Part 4 (dispute resolution processes) does not apply in relation to a proceeding for review of the decision.
When this section applies
This section applies in relation to an intelligence and security decision.
Guidance and appeals panel
Part 5 (guidance and appeals panel) does not apply in relation to:
an application for review of the decision; or
a decision of the Tribunal on review of the decision.

section.heading: Duty of Tribunal in relation to security and law enforcement information

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding in the Intelligence and Security jurisdictional area.
Duty to protect security and law enforcement information

It is the duty of the Tribunal, even though there may be no relevant certificate under this or any other Act, to ensure, so far as possible, that information is not communicated or made available to a person if that communication or availability would prejudice:
the security, defence or international relations of the Commonwealth; or
law enforcement or intelligence interests.

section.heading: Restricting publication or disclosure of information

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies:
in relation to a proceeding in the Intelligence and Security jurisdictional area; and
in addition to:
section 70 (Tribunal may restrict publication or disclosure of information); and
section 71 (requirements for Tribunal orders about hearings, publication and disclosure).
Orders restricting publication or disclosure of information
In considering whether to make an order under section 70 restricting publication or other disclosure of information, the Tribunal must:
in any case—have regard to the necessity of avoiding the disclosure of national security information; and
if the proceeding is for review of an intelligence and security decision—give particular weight to any submission made by, or on behalf of, the agency head.
Orders restricting publication or disclosure of findings
The Tribunal may, by order, give directions prohibiting or restricting the publication or other disclosure of the whole or any part of its findings in the proceeding.
Note: Breach of a non-publication or non-disclosure order is an offence (see section 119).
When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding for review of an intelligence and security decision, other than an exempt security record decision.
This section applies in relation to evidence to be adduced or a submission to be made by or on behalf of any of the following:
the agency head;
a relevant body;
an officer or employee of the agency head’s agency;
an officer or employee of a relevant body;
a person connected with the agency or a relevant body.
Security certificates by responsible Ministers
The responsible Minister may certify, in writing, that disclosing the evidence or making the submission would be contrary to the public interest because it would prejudice:
in any case—the security, defence or international relations of the Commonwealth; or
in the case of a criminal intelligence assessment decision—law enforcement or intelligence interests.
If the responsible Minister so certifies, when the evidence is adduced or the submission is made:
the applicant must not be present; and
the applicant’s representative must not be present except with the consent of the responsible Minister.
A certificate under this section is not a legislative instrument.
Delegation—security clearance decisions and security clearance suitability assessments
The ASIO Minister may, in writing, delegate the ASIO Minister’s power under subsection (3) in relation to a security clearance decision or a security clearance suitability assessment to:
the Director-General of Security; or

an ASIO employee (within the meaning of the ASIO Act), or an ASIO affiliate (within the meaning of that Act), who holds, or is acting in, a position in ASIO that is equivalent to or higher than a position occupied by an SES employee.
In exercising a power under the delegation, the delegate must comply with any written directions of the ASIO Minister.
Offence
An applicant’s representative commits an offence if:
a certificate is given under subsection (3) in relation to evidence or a submission; and
the representative is present when the evidence is adduced or the submission is made; and
the representative discloses the evidence, or any information that was part of the submission, to the applicant or to any other person.
Penalty: Imprisonment for 2 years.
When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding for review of:
a security clearance decision; or
a security clearance suitability assessment.
Sensitive information certificates

(2) The Director-General of Security or a person authorised by the Director-General under this section may certify, in writing, that, in the opinion of the Director-General or authorised person, disclosure of information (the sensitive information) contained in a document given to the Tribunal by the Director-General in relation to a proceeding:
would be contrary to the public interest for one or more of the following reasons:
the disclosure would prejudice the security, defence or international relations of the Commonwealth;
the disclosure would reveal information that has been disclosed to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation in confidence;

any other reason that could form the basis for a claim by the Crown in right of the Commonwealth in a judicial proceeding that the sensitive information or the matter contained in the document should not be disclosed; or
could reveal the methodology underlying a psychological assessment of the person who applied for the decision or assessment.
A certificate under subsection (2) is not a legislative instrument.
Effect of certificate
If a certificate is given under subsection (2), the Tribunal must do all things necessary to ensure that the sensitive information is not disclosed to the applicant or any person other than:
the Director-General of Security or the Director-General’s representative; or
a member in the course of the performance of the member’s duties; or
the Principal Registrar in the course of the performance of the Principal Registrar’s duties; or
a staff member in the course of the performance of the staff member’s duties.
However, subsection (4) does not apply in relation to disclosure to the applicant or a person representing the applicant to the extent that the information:
has already been lawfully disclosed to the applicant; or
is disclosed to the applicant with the consent of the Director-General of Security.
Authorisations

The Director-General of Security may, in writing, authorise a person for the purposes of this section if the person is an ASIO employee (within the meaning of the ASIO Act), or an ASIO affiliate (within the meaning of that Act), who holds, or is acting in, a position in ASIO that is equivalent to or higher than a position occupied by an SES employee.

section.heading: Protecting identities of persons giving evidence

content.p: When this section applies
This section applies in relation to a proceeding in the Intelligence and Security jurisdictional area.
Protecting identities
The Tribunal must do all things necessary to ensure that the identity of a person is not revealed if:
the person gives, or is to give, evidence on behalf of an agency within the national intelligence community; and
the head of the agency requests that the identity of the person is not revealed.
When this section applies
This section applies:
in relation to a proceeding for review of an intelligence and security decision, other than an exempt security record decision; and
instead of the following provisions:
section 91 (disclosure of information—public interest certificate);
section 92 (Attorney-General may intervene for public interest reasons);
section 112 (notice of decision and statement of reasons—other proceedings) to the extent that it would apply in relation anything done under this section.
Public interest certificate

The responsible Minister may certify, in writing, that the disclosure of specified information, or the content of a specified document, in the proceeding would be contrary to the public interest for one or more of the following reasons:
the disclosure would prejudice the security, defence or international relations of the Commonwealth;
the disclosure would involve the disclosure of deliberations or decisions of the Cabinet or of a Committee of the Cabinet;
if the proceeding is for review of a criminal intelligence assessment—the disclosure would prejudice law enforcement or intelligence interests;

any other reason that could form the basis for a claim by the Crown in right of the Commonwealth in a judicial proceeding that the information or the matter contained in the document should not be disclosed.
A certificate under subsection (2) is not a legislative instrument.
Effect of certificate

If a certificate is given under subsection (2) in relation to information or a document, a person is not excused from disclosing the information, or giving the document, to the Tribunal for the purposes of the proceeding if the person is required by or under this Act to do so.
However, the Tribunal must do all things necessary to ensure that:
subject to subsection (6), the information or document is not disclosed or given to any person other than:
a member in the course of the performance of the member’s duties; or
the Principal Registrar in the course of the performance of the Principal Registrar’s duties; or
a staff member in the course of the performance of the staff member’s duties; and

in the case of a document given to the Tribunal by an agency head—the document is returned, to the agency from which it came, as soon as practicable after the Tribunal has finished considering the document.
Tribunal may allow disclosure in limited cases

The Tribunal may decide to make the information or document available to any or all of the parties to the proceeding if the certificate does not specify the reason set out in paragraph (2)(a), (b) or (c).
In deciding whether to make the information or document available, the Tribunal must:

take into account as a primary consideration the principle that it is desirable, in the interest of ensuring the effective performance of the Tribunal’s functions, for the parties to the proceeding to be made aware of all relevant matters; and
have regard to any reason specified in the certificate.
Responsible Minister is party to proceeding
The responsible Minister is a party to the proceeding if:
the certificate does not specify a reason set out in paragraph (2)(a), (b) or (c); and
the responsible Minister would not otherwise be a party to the proceeding.
Notice of public interest decisions
If the Tribunal decides to make the information or document available under subsection (6), the Tribunal must, as soon as practicable, give each party to the proceeding reasons for the decision.
Exclusion of other laws

This section excludes the operation of any other law that relates to the public interest and would otherwise apply in relation to the disclosure of information, or of the content of documents, in a proceeding in the Tribunal.
Delegation—security clearance decisions and security clearance suitability assessments
The ASIO Minister may, in writing, delegate the ASIO Minister’s power under subsection (2) in relation to a security clearance decision or a security clearance suitability assessment to:
the Director-General of Security; or

an ASIO employee (within the meaning of the ASIO Act), or an ASIO affiliate (within the meaning of that Act), who holds, or is acting in, a position in ASIO that is equivalent to or higher than a position occupied by an SES employee.
In exercising a power under the delegation, the delegate must comply with any written directions of the ASIO Minister.
When this section applies

This section applies in relation to a proceeding for review of a decision mentioned in column 1 of an item in the following table if a certificate made under the provision mentioned in column 2 of the item has been given in relation to the decision.

content.p: Effect of certificate
The certificate does not excuse a person from disclosing information, or giving a document, to the Tribunal for the purposes of the proceeding if the person is required by or under this Act to do so.
However, the Tribunal must do all things necessary to ensure that:
the information or document is not disclosed or given to any person other than:
a member in the course of the performance of the member’s duties; or
the Principal Registrar in the course of the performance of the Principal Registrar’s duties; or
a staff member in the course of the performance of the staff member’s duties; and

in the case of a document given to the Tribunal by an agency head—the document is returned, to the agency from which it came, as soon as practicable after the Tribunal has finished considering the document.
Subdivision A—Limits on certain decisions
When this section applies
This section applies:
in relation to the review of a security clearance decision; and
instead of the following provisions:
section 105 (Tribunal decision on review of reviewable decision);
section 112 (notice of decision and statement of reasons—other proceedings).
Possible decisions
The Tribunal must make a decision:
affirming the security clearance decision; or
setting aside the security clearance decision and remitting the matter to the decision-maker for reconsideration in accordance with any orders or recommendations of the Tribunal.
When Tribunal’s decision on review comes into operation
However, section 107 (when Tribunal’s decision on review comes into operation) applies as if the Tribunal’s decision on the review were made under section 105.
Subdivision B—Recording and communicating decisions
This Subdivision applies:
in relation to the review of an intelligence and security decision other than an exempt security record decision; and
instead of section 111 (notice of decision and statement of reasons—review of reviewable decision).
The Tribunal:
must make and record its findings in relation to the decision; and
in relation to those findings—may state the opinion of the Tribunal as to the correctness of, or justification for, any opinion, advice or information contained in the decision.

The Tribunal must not make findings in relation to the decision that would have the effect of superseding any information that is (or is taken to be) part of the decision unless those findings state that, in the Tribunal’s opinion, the information:
is incorrect; or
is incorrectly represented; or
could not reasonably be relevant to the requirements of security; or
could not reasonably be relevant for the purposes of having regard to whether there is intelligence or information that suggests that the person:
may commit a serious and organised crime; or
may assist another person to commit a serious and organised crime.
Written notice of decisions and findings
The Tribunal must give written notice of its decision on the review, and copies of its findings made under section 166, to:
the applicant; and
the agency head; and
the responsible Minister.
The notice must include notice of the right of the party to appeal to the Federal Court under Division 2 of Part 7.
The agency head must give the notice and findings to each relevant body.
Oral notice of decisions and findings
The Tribunal may give its decision and findings orally before giving them in writing.
Directions about disclosure

The Tribunal may, by order, direct that the whole or a particular part of its findings, so far as they relate to a matter that has not already been disclosed to the applicant, is not to be given to the applicant or a relevant body.
Time for giving written notice and findings

The written notice and findings must be given by the time specified in the practice directions. If the practice directions do not specify a time, the written notice and findings must be given within 28 days after the day the Tribunal’s decision is made.
Effect of failure to comply
A failure to comply with this section does not affect the validity of the Tribunal’s decision.
Effect of non-disclosure provisions
To avoid doubt, this section is subject to other provisions of this Part that prohibit or restrict the disclosure of information or documents.

section.heading: Findings relating to procedures or practices of agency

content.p: The Tribunal may provide, with the findings given to the agency head and the responsible Minister, any comments the Tribunal wishes to make on matters relating to procedures or practices of the agency that have come to the Tribunal’s attention as a result of the review.
Subject to any order of the Tribunal, the applicant is entitled to publish the following, in any manner the applicant thinks fit:
the Tribunal’s decision on the review;
the findings of the Tribunal so far as they have been given to the applicant.

part.heading: Appeals and references of questions of law to Federal Court

content.p: A party to a proceeding in the Tribunal may appeal to the Federal Court, on a question of law, from the decision of the Tribunal in the proceeding. A decision that a person’s interests are not affected by a reviewable decision may also be appealed. Timeframes apply to making appeals, but may be extended. An appeal does not affect the operation of a Tribunal decision unless the Court orders otherwise.
This Part contains the standard provisions for how the Court operates when dealing with an appeal. Other legislation can include provisions that apply in addition to, or instead of, these provisions.
The Federal Court may transfer some kinds of appeal to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2).
There are provisions facilitating remittal of matters to the Tribunal to be decided again.
In some circumstances, the Tribunal may refer a question of law to the Federal Court.
There are requirements (including some non-disclosure obligations) relating to sending documents between the Tribunal and the courts.

section.heading: Part applies whether Tribunal’s power is conferred by Commonwealth, State or Territory law

content.p: This Part applies in relation to a proceeding before the Tribunal under power conferred on it by or under:
an Act or an instrument made under an Act; or
a law of a State, the Australian Capital Territory or the Northern Territory.

This Part has effect in relation to a proceeding before the Tribunal under power conferred on it by or under a law of a State, the Australian Capital Territory or the Northern Territory as if a reference in this Part to a provision of this Act that is not in this Part were a reference to that provision as applying as a law of the State or Territory.
Subdivision A—Appeals on questions of law
A party to a proceeding in the Tribunal may appeal to the Federal Court, on a question of law, from the decision of the Tribunal in the proceeding.

Note 1: A party to a proceeding for review of a decision of the Child Support Registrar, or second review that relates to the decision, may in some instances appeal instead to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) (see section 99 of the Child Support (Registration and Collection) Act 1988 and section 131E of this Act).

Note 2: For when a party to a proceeding for review of a decision under the Migration Act 1958 can make an application to the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2), see sections 476 and 476A of the Migration Act 1958).
To avoid doubt, subsection (1) does not apply in relation to a decision under section 128 (President decides whether to refer Tribunal decision to guidance and appeals panel).
Note: A decision under section 128 is not a decision of the Tribunal.
A person may appeal to the Federal Court from a decision of the Tribunal that the person’s interests are not affected by a reviewable decision.

section.heading: Time and manner for making appeals

content.p: The appeal must be made:
if either of the following applies—no later than 28 days after the Tribunal gives the party or person its statement of reasons for the decision:
the Tribunal is required to give a statement of reasons for the decision;
the party or person has a right to request a statement of reasons for the decision and exercises the right; or

if the party or person has a right to request a statement of reasons for the decision and does not exercise the right—no later than 28 days after the last day on which the party or person could have requested a statement of reasons for the decision; or
in any other case—no later than 28 days after the party or person is given the decision.
However, the Federal Court may extend the period within which the appeal must be made.

For the purposes of counting the 28 days mentioned in paragraphs (1)(a), (b) and (c), do not take into account any day in the period starting on 24 December in a year and ending on 14 January in the next year.

If a person applies to refer the decision to the guidance and appeals panel, for the purposes of counting the 28 days mentioned in paragraph (1)(a), (b) or (c), do not take into account any day in the period between the day the application is made and the day the President refers the decision or refuses the application.
(4) The appeal must be made in the manner prescribed by the Rules of Court made under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976.
The appeal must be heard by a Full Court if the decision is given by:
a member who is a Judge; or
the Tribunal constituted for the purposes of a proceeding by a member who is, or members at least one of whom is, a Judge.
The appeal may be heard by a Full Court if:
subsection (1) does not apply; and
the decision is given by:
a member who is a Non-Judicial Deputy President; or
the Tribunal constituted for the purposes of a proceeding by a member who is, or members at least one of whom is, a Non-Judicial Deputy President; or
the Tribunal constituted for the purposes of a proceeding by the guidance and appeals panel; and
the Chief Justice of the Court, following consultation with the President, thinks it appropriate.
Subdivision B—Jurisdiction and powers of Federal Court
If an appeal is made under Subdivision A, the Federal Court:
has jurisdiction to hear and determine the appeal; and
must hear and determine the appeal; and
may make any order it considers appropriate because of its decision.
Without limiting the orders it may make, the Federal Court may:
affirm or set aside a decision of the Tribunal; or
remit a matter to be decided again by the Tribunal, either with or without the taking of further evidence, in accordance with the directions of the Court.

section.heading: Court may make findings of fact

content.p: In hearing the appeal, the Federal Court may make findings of fact if:
the findings of fact are not inconsistent with findings of fact made by the Tribunal (other than findings made by the Tribunal as the result of an error of law); and
it appears to the Court that it is convenient to do so.
In deciding whether it is convenient, the Court must have regard to:
the extent (if any) to which it is necessary to make findings of fact; and
the means by which those facts might be established; and
the quick and efficient resolution of the whole of the matter; and
the relative expense and delay (if any) to the parties if the Court, rather than the Tribunal, makes the findings of fact; and
whether any of the parties considers that it is appropriate for the Court, rather than the Tribunal, to make the findings of fact; and
any other matters that the Court considers relevant.
For the purposes of this section, the Court may:
have regard to the evidence given in the proceeding in the Tribunal; and
receive further evidence.

section.heading: Operation and implementation of Tribunal’s decision

content.p: General rule—operation or implementation not affected
An appeal to the Federal Court from a decision of the Tribunal does not affect the operation of the decision or prevent the taking of action to implement the decision.
Exception—Court may stay operation or implementation

However, for the purpose of ensuring the effectiveness of the hearing and determination of the appeal, the Court or a Judge of the Court may make an order staying or otherwise affecting the operation or implementation of either or both of the following:
the decision of the Tribunal, or a part of that decision;
the reviewable decision to which the decision of the Tribunal relates, or a part of that reviewable decision.
The order is subject to any conditions specified in the order.
The order remains in force until the decision on the appeal is given.
Despite subsection (4), if:
the order states that it applies for a period; and
the period ends before the decision on the appeal is given;
the order has effect until the end of the period.
The order may be varied or revoked by the Court or a Judge of the Court.

division.heading: Transfer of appeals to Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2)

content.p: General rule—Federal Court may transfer appeal
If an appeal under Subdivision A of Division 2 is pending in the Federal Court, the Federal Court may, by order, transfer the appeal to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2).
The Federal Court may do so:
on the application of a party to the appeal; or
on its own initiative.
Matters to which Federal Court must have regard
In deciding whether to transfer the appeal, the Federal Court must have regard to the following:
any Rules of Court made for the purposes of section 181;
whether proceedings in respect of an associated matter are pending in the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2);
whether the resources of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) are sufficient to hear and determine the appeal;
the interests of the administration of justice.
Jurisdiction and powers of Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2)

If the Federal Court transfers the appeal, Subdivision B of Division 2 (jurisdiction and powers of Federal Court) applies in relation to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) in the same way as it applies in relation to the Federal Court.
Exception—certain appeals must not be transferred
However, the Federal Court must not transfer the appeal if it:
relates to a decision given by the Tribunal constituted by a member who is, or by members at least one of whom is, a Judge or a Non-Judicial Deputy President; or
is of a kind prescribed by the rules.

section.heading: No appeal from decision to transfer

content.p: No appeal lies in relation to a decision of the Federal Court to transfer an appeal under this Division.
(1) Rules of Court made under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 may make provision in relation to the transfer of appeals under this Division.
In particular, the Rules of Court may set out factors that are to be taken into account in deciding whether to transfer an appeal.
Before Rules of Court are made for the purposes of this section, the Federal Court must consult the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2).
This Division applies if:
an appeal is made to the Federal Court from a decision of the Tribunal; and
either:
the Federal Court remits the matter to the Tribunal to be decided again; or
if the Federal Court transfers the appeal to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2)—that court remits the matter to the Tribunal to be decided again.
The Tribunal does not need to be constituted for the review by the person or persons who made the decision.
To avoid doubt, constituting the Tribunal for the review is not a reconstitution for the purposes of Subdivision D of Division 4 of Part 4 (reconstitution).

section.heading: Tribunal may rely on previous proceedings

content.p: The Tribunal may have regard to:
any record of the proceeding in the Tribunal prior to the appeal (including a record of any evidence taken in the proceeding); and
any document or thing relating to the proceeding given to the Tribunal prior to the appeal;
unless doing so would be inconsistent with the directions of the court.
The Tribunal may, with the agreement of the President, refer a question of law arising in a proceeding in the Tribunal to the Federal Court for decision.
The Tribunal may do so:
at the request of a party to the proceeding; or
on its own initiative.
The Federal Court has jurisdiction to hear and determine a question of law referred to it under this section.
If, after consulting the President, the Chief Justice of the Court considers it appropriate, that jurisdiction is to be exercised by the Court constituted as a Full Court.
If a question of law arising in any proceeding has been referred to the Federal Court under this section, the Tribunal must not, in that proceeding:
give a decision to which the question is relevant while the reference is pending; or
proceed in a manner, or make a decision, that is inconsistent with the opinion of the Court on the question.
This Division applies if:
a party to a proceeding in the Tribunal appeals to the Federal Court from a decision of the Tribunal (see sections 172 and 173); or
the Tribunal refers a question of law arising in a proceeding to the Federal Court (see section 185).
The Tribunal must send to the Federal Court all documents that:
were before the Tribunal in connection with the proceeding; and
are relevant to the appeal or reference.
If the Federal Court transfers an appeal to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2):
the Federal Court must send the documents concerned to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2); and

sections 189 (disclosure contrary to public interest) and 190 (disclosure of security clearance documents) apply in relation to that court in the same way as they apply in relation to the Federal Court.
To avoid doubt, paragraph (2)(a) has effect despite:
section 91 (disclosure of information—public interest certificate); and
any provision of Part 6 (proceedings in Intelligence and Security jurisdictional area); or
a certificate made under a provision mentioned in column 2 of the table in subsection 162(1) (non-disclosure certificates under other Acts); or
section 272 (public interest certificate in relation to statement of reasons).
At the conclusion of the proceeding before the Federal Court in relation to the appeal or reference, the Court must return to the Tribunal the documents sent to the Court under this Division.

However, if the Federal Court sends the documents to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2), the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) must return the documents to the Tribunal at the conclusion of the proceeding before the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) in relation to the appeal or reference.
When this section applies
This section applies if:
a document is sent to the Federal Court under this Division; and
a certificate in force under one of the following provisions certifies that disclosure of a matter contained in the document would be contrary to the public interest:
subsection 91(1) or (2) (disclosure of information—public interest certificate);
subsection 161(2) (public interest certificates—responsible Minister);
a provision mentioned in column 2 of the table in subsection 162(1) (non-disclosure certificates under other Acts);
subsection 272(1) (public interest certificate in relation to statement of reasons).
General rule
The Federal Court must do all things necessary to ensure that the matter is not disclosed to any person other than a member of the court as constituted for the purposes of the appeal or reference.
Exception
However, the Federal Court must permit the parties to the proceeding in the Tribunal to inspect the part of the document that contains the matter if:
the document is covered by a certificate mentioned in paragraph (b); and
a reason specified in the certificate in relation to the matter is not a reason mentioned in:
for a certificate in force under subsection 91(1)—paragraph 91(1)(a) or (b); or
for a certificate in force under subsection 91(2)—paragraph 91(2)(a); or
for a certificate in force under subsection 161(2)—paragraph 161(2)(a), (b) or (c); or
for a certificate in force under subsection 272(1)—paragraph 272(1)(a) or (b); and
a question for decision by the Court is whether the matter should be disclosed to some or all of the parties to the proceeding in the Tribunal; and
the Court decides that the matter should be so disclosed.
When this section applies
This section applies if a document sent to the Federal Court under this Division:
is a copy of a standard (or part of a standard) mentioned in subsection 143(1); or
contains sensitive information as mentioned in subsection 159(2).
General rule

The Federal Court must do all things necessary to ensure that the copy of the standard (or part) and any information contained in it, or the sensitive information, is not disclosed to any person other than:
a member of the court as constituted for the purposes of the proceeding; or
the Director-General of Security or the Director-General’s representative.
Exception

However, subsection (2) does not apply in relation to a disclosure to the person who was the applicant, or a person representing the person who was the applicant, in the proceeding in the Tribunal to the extent that the information:
has already been lawfully disclosed to the person; or
is disclosed to the person with the consent of the Director-General of Security.

section.heading: Disclosure to officers of the court

content.p: Nothing in this Division prevents the disclosure of a document, information or a matter contained in a document to an officer of a court who is performing duties as such an officer.

The Tribunal has different jurisdictional areas. Lists may be established as sub-areas within jurisdictional areas. The President, or some Non-Judicial Deputy Presidents, may lead a jurisdictional area. A Deputy President or senior member may lead a list. Members may be assigned to one or more jurisdictional areas.

Members of the Tribunal have different functions and obligations. Generally, before a person is appointed as a member (other than a Judicial Deputy President) the Minister must be satisfied that the person was assessed as suitable for the appointment through a merit-based assessment process.

The President must determine a code of conduct and performance standard for non-judicial members. The President may investigate some conduct of non-judicial members, and must notify the Minister if the President reasonably believes there are grounds for termination of a non-judicial member.

One of the President’s functions is to inform relevant Ministers, relevant Commonwealth entities and the Council of identified systemic issues. Jurisdictional area leaders are to inform the President of systemic issues identified in relation to their jurisdictional areas.
The President is responsible for managing the administrative affairs of the Tribunal.
The Principal Registrar’s functions include:
assisting the President in managing the administrative affairs of the Tribunal; and
providing the corporate and registry services of the Tribunal.
There are provisions related to the terms and conditions on which members and the Principal Registrar hold office.
The Tribunal Advisory Committee is established. The Committee consists of the President, the Principal Registrar, the jurisdictional area leaders and other nominated members.
The staff of the Tribunal must be persons engaged under the Public Service Act 1999. Staff members may be appointed as registrars.
Subdivision A—Members and functions
The President has the following functions:
to participate as a member of the Tribunal, particularly in proceedings involving complex, significant or sensitive matters;
if assigned under section 197 to be a jurisdictional area leader—to perform the functions of a jurisdictional area leader;
to manage the business of the Tribunal;
to manage the performance and conduct of members;
to ensure that the Tribunal operates efficiently and effectively and continually pursues the objective in section 9;
to provide intellectual leadership to the Tribunal, including by promoting best practice in decision-making by the Tribunal;
to provide leadership and guidance to, and engender cohesiveness and collaboration among, members and staff members;
to promote the training, education and professional development of members;

to inform relevant Ministers, relevant Commonwealth entities and the Council of any systemic issues related to the making of reviewable decisions that have been identified in the caseload of the Tribunal;
any other functions conferred on the President by this Act or another Act;
to engage with civil society in relation to the performance of any of the above functions;
to do anything incidental or conducive to the performance of any of the above functions.
Judicial Deputy President
A Judicial Deputy President has the following functions:
to participate as a member of the Tribunal, particularly in proceedings involving complex, significant or sensitive matters;
to ensure that the Tribunal continually pursues the objective in section 9;
to provide intellectual leadership to the Tribunal, including by promoting best practice in decision-making by the Tribunal;
any other functions conferred on a Judicial Deputy President by this Act or another Act;
to do anything incidental or conducive to the performance of any of the above functions.
Non-Judicial Deputy President
A Non-Judicial Deputy President has the following functions:
to participate as a member of the Tribunal, particularly in proceedings involving complex, significant or sensitive matters;
to ensure that the Tribunal continually pursues the objective in section 9;
to provide intellectual leadership to the Tribunal, including by promoting best practice in decision-making by the Tribunal;
to assist the President in the performance of the President’s functions;
if assigned under section 197 to be a jurisdictional area leader—to perform the functions of a jurisdictional area leader;
any other functions conferred on a Non-Judicial Deputy President by this Act or another Act;
to do anything incidental or conducive to the performance of any of the above functions.

section.heading: Functions of senior and general members

content.p: Senior members
A senior member has the following functions:
to participate as a member of the Tribunal, particularly in proceedings involving more complex matters;
to assist each jurisdictional area leader of each jurisdictional area to which the senior member has been assigned in the performance of the jurisdictional area leader’s functions;
to promote best practice in decision-making by the Tribunal;
any other functions conferred on a senior member by this Act or another Act;
to do anything incidental or conducive to the performance of any of the above functions.
General members
A general member has the following functions:
to participate as a member of the Tribunal;
any other functions conferred on a general member by this Act or another Act;
to do anything incidental or conducive to the performance of any of the above functions.
Subdivision B—Jurisdictional areas and lists
The following jurisdictional areas of the Tribunal are established:
General;
Intelligence and Security;
Migration;
National Disability Insurance Scheme;
Protection;
Social Security;
Taxation and Business;
Veterans’ and Workers’ Compensation.
The President:
may establish one or more lists as subareas within a jurisdictional area; and
may abolish any such list.
Before establishing or abolishing a list, the President must consult the Tribunal Advisory Committee.
The Tribunal’s powers in relation to a proceeding are to be exercised in the jurisdictional area or list that the President directs.
If a direction is made in writing, the direction is not a legislative instrument.
Assignment of jurisdictional area leaders
The Minister may, in consultation with the President, assign either or both of the following to be a leader of one or more jurisdictional areas:
the President;
a Non-Judicial Deputy President appointed on a salaried basis.
The Minister may, on the recommendation of the President, vary or revoke an assignment under subsection (1).
The President must not make a recommendation to the Minister to vary or revoke an assignment under subsection (1) unless:
the assignment has been in effect for more than 6 months; and
the President is satisfied that the variation or revocation would meet the operational needs of the Tribunal.
If an assignment under subsection (1) is made in writing, the assignment is not a legislative instrument.
Functions of jurisdictional area leaders
A jurisdictional area leader has the following functions:
to provide intellectual leadership to members assigned to the jurisdictional area, including by promoting best practice in decision-making by those members;
to assist the President to ensure that the Tribunal operates efficiently and effectively and continually pursues the objective in section 9 across all jurisdictional areas;
to oversee, and respond to issues and trends in, the caseload strategy of the jurisdictional area in consultation with the President;
to assist the President to manage the performance and conduct of members assigned to the jurisdictional area;
to provide training, education and professional development opportunities to members assigned to the jurisdictional area;
to identify systemic issues related to the making of reviewable decisions arising in the caseload of the jurisdictional area and to inform the President of those issues.
Acting jurisdictional area leaders

The Minister may, in consultation with the President, assign a Non-Judicial Deputy President appointed on a salaried basis or a senior member appointed on a salaried basis to act, for a period of no more than 3 months, as a jurisdictional area leader in relation to a jurisdictional area:
during a vacancy in the position of a jurisdictional area leader in relation to the jurisdictional area (whether or not an assignment has previously been made to the position); or
during any period, or during all periods, when a jurisdictional area leader in relation to the jurisdictional area:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the position.
Note: For rules that apply to a person acting as a jurisdictional area leader, see section 33A of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.

section.heading: Assignment of members to lead lists

content.p: Assignments
The President may assign a Deputy President or senior member to lead one or more lists.
Subject to subsection (4), the President may vary or revoke an assignment under subsection (1).
Acting assignments
The President may assign a Deputy President or senior member to act as the leader of a list:
during a vacancy in the position of leader of that list (whether or not an assignment has previously been made to the position); or
during any period, or during all periods, when the leader of that list:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the position.
Note: For rules that apply to a person acting as the leader of a list, see section 33A of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.
Consultation

The President must not make, vary or revoke an assignment under subsection (1) or (3) unless the President has consulted each jurisdictional area leader of each list affected by the making, variation or revocation.
Assignment not a legislative instrument
If an assignment under subsection (1) or (3) is made in writing, the assignment is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Assignment of members to jurisdictional areas

content.p: Deputy Presidents
A Deputy President is assigned to every jurisdictional area.
Senior member leading a list
A senior member assigned to lead a list is assigned to the jurisdictional area within which the list is established.
Assignment by President
The President may, in writing, assign a member (other than the President or a Deputy President) to one or more jurisdictional areas.
However, the President must not do so if an assignment under subsection (8) in relation to the member has been made and has not been revoked.
Before assigning a member to a jurisdictional area, the President must be satisfied that the member has the appropriate skills, qualifications and experience.
The President may vary or revoke an assignment under subsection (3) at any time.
An assignment under subsection (3) is not a legislative instrument.
Assignment by Governor-General

The Governor-General may, on the recommendation of the Minister, assign a member (other than the President or a Deputy President) to one or more jurisdictional areas by specifying the assignment in the member’s instrument of appointment.
However, the Governor-General must not do so if an assignment under subsection (8) in relation to the member has been made and has been revoked.
Before the Governor-General assigns a member to a jurisdictional area, the Minister must be satisfied that:
there are exceptional circumstances that justify the assignment; and
the member has the appropriate skills, qualifications and experience.
The Governor-General may at any time, by varying a member’s instrument of appointment:
assign the member to one or more additional jurisdictional areas; or
revoke the member’s assignment to each of the jurisdictional areas.

section.heading: President may give directions to members

content.p: The President may give a written direction to a non-judicial member relating to the performance of the member’s duties.
The member must comply with the direction.
A direction given under subsection (1):
must be consistent with the President’s functions; and
must not relate to a particular proceeding in the Tribunal.
A direction under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.
The President must, in writing, determine a code of conduct for non-judicial members.
Note: A serious breach of the code of conduct may lead to termination of a non-judicial member’s appointment (see section 221).

Without limiting subsection (1), the code of conduct must make provision for the taking of action by the President or a jurisdictional area leader in relation to non-judicial members upholding the code of conduct.
Subsection (1) does not limit section 36 (President may make practice directions).
The President must publish the code of conduct.
The code of conduct is not a legislative instrument.
The President must, in writing, determine a performance standard for non-judicial members.
Note: A serious breach of the performance standard may lead to termination of a non-judicial member’s appointment (see section 221).

Without limiting subsection (1), the performance standard must make provision for the taking of action by the President or a jurisdictional area leader in relation to non-judicial members meeting the performance standard.
Subsection (1) does not limit section 36 (President may make practice directions).
The President must publish the performance standard.
The performance standard is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: President may investigate conduct of members

content.p: This section applies if the President forms the opinion that a non-judicial member may have engaged in conduct that:
may constitute a breach of the code of conduct; or
may constitute a breach of the performance standard; or
may constitute a ground for terminating the appointment of the member in accordance with section 221; or
may adversely affect, or may have adversely affected, the performance of official duties by the member; or
may adversely affect, or may have adversely affected, public trust and confidence in the Tribunal.
Note: For example, the President may form the opinion because of a complaint made to the Tribunal in relation to the conduct.
The President may:
do one or more of the following:
investigate the conduct;
report on an investigation of the conduct;
deal with a report of an investigation of the conduct;
refer the conduct to a person or body;
direct a person or body to investigate the conduct;
authorise, in writing, a person or body to do any of the above;
take any measures in relation to the member that the President believes are reasonably necessary to maintain public trust and confidence in the Tribunal; or
take no action, or no further action, in relation to the conduct.
Note 1: The President is also required to notify the Minister if the President reasonably believes that there are grounds for terminating the member’s appointment under section 221 (see section 222).
Note 2: For protections for persons involved in investigating conduct of members, see section 204.

The President may, at any time after forming the opinion mentioned in subsection (1), temporarily restrict the member’s duties if the President reasonably believes that doing so is in the public, or the Tribunal’s, interest.

section.heading: Protection of persons involved in investigating conduct of members etc.

content.p: A person who is performing or exercising functions or powers under or for the purposes of section 203 in relation to conduct that was, or may have been, engaged in by a member, or assisting in performing or exercising those functions or powers, has the same protection and immunity as a Justice of the High Court.

A person appearing before a person who is performing or exercising functions or powers under or for the purposes of section 203 in relation to conduct that was, or may have been, engaged in by a member has the same protection, and is subject to the same liabilities, as a witness in proceedings in the High Court.

A legal practitioner assisting, or appearing on behalf of a person before, a person who is performing or exercising functions or powers for the purposes of section 203 in relation to conduct that was, or may have been, engaged in by a member has the same protection and immunity as a barrister appearing for a party in proceedings in the High Court.
Subdivision A—Appointment of members
Appointment by Governor-General
The President is to be appointed by the Governor-General, by written instrument, on the recommendation of the Minister.
Before the Minister makes a recommendation to the Governor-General, the Minister must:
consult the Chief Justice of the Federal Court; and
be satisfied that the person was assessed, by a panel established under section 209, as suitable for the appointment through an assessment process that:
was merit-based; and
included public advertising of the position; and
complied with the requirements (if any) prescribed by the regulations.
Qualification for appointment
A person must not be appointed as the President unless the person is a Judge of the Federal Court.
Period of appointment
The President holds office for a period of 5 years unless a shorter period is specified in the instrument of appointment.
If the instrument of appointment specifies a shorter period, the instrument must state the reasons why the shorter period is specified.
Basis of appointment
The President must be appointed on a salaried basis.
Reappointment
A person may be reappointed as the President by written instrument made within 6 months before the end of the period specified in the person’s instrument of appointment.

Paragraph (2)(b) does not apply in relation to the reappointment of a person who, immediately before the start of the period of reappointment, holds office as the President under a previous appointment under subsection (1).
Appointment by Governor-General
A Judicial Deputy President is to be appointed by the Governor-General, by written instrument, on the recommendation of the Minister.
Before the Minister makes a recommendation to the Governor-General, the Minister must:
consult the Chief Justice of the court of which the person is a Judge; and
seek, and take into account, the advice of the President in relation to:
whether the appointment would meet the operational needs of the Tribunal; and
the effect of the appointment on the number of Judicial Deputy Presidents relative to the number of Non-Judicial Deputy Presidents, senior members and general members.
Qualification for appointment
A person must not be appointed as a Judicial Deputy President unless the person is:
a Judge of the Federal Court; or
a Judge of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1).
Period of appointment
A Judicial Deputy President holds office for a period of 5 years unless a shorter period is specified in the instrument of appointment.
If the instrument of appointment specifies a shorter period, the instrument must state the reasons why the shorter period is specified.
Basis of appointment
A Judicial Deputy President must be appointed on a sessional basis.
Appointment by Governor-General
A Non-Judicial Deputy President is to be appointed by the Governor-General, by written instrument, on the recommendation of the Minister.
Before the Minister makes a recommendation to the Governor-General, the Minister must:
seek, and take into account, the advice of the President in relation to:
whether the appointment would meet the operational needs of the Tribunal; and
the financial capacity of the Tribunal for the appointment; and
the effect of the appointment on the number of Non-Judicial Deputy Presidents relative to the number of senior members and general members; and
be satisfied that the person was assessed, by a panel established under section 209, as suitable for the appointment through an assessment process that:
was merit-based; and
included public advertising of the position; and
complied with the requirements (if any) prescribed by the regulations.
Qualification for appointment
A person must not be appointed as a Non-Judicial Deputy President unless:
the person is enrolled as a legal practitioner and has been so enrolled for at least 10 years; and
either:
the person is a former Judge; or
the Minister is satisfied that the person has substantial expertise in one or more areas relevant to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.
Period of appointment
A Non-Judicial Deputy President holds office for a period of 5 years unless a shorter period is specified in the instrument of appointment.
If the instrument of appointment specifies a shorter period, the instrument must state the reasons why the shorter period is specified.
Basis of appointment
A Non-Judicial Deputy President may be appointed on a salaried or sessional basis.
Reappointment
A person may be reappointed as a Non-Judicial Deputy President by written instrument made within 6 months before the end of the period specified in the person’s instrument of appointment.

Before a person is reappointed as a Non-Judicial Deputy President, the Minister must seek, and take into account, the advice of the President in relation to the person’s performance against the performance standard.
Paragraph (2)(b) applies only in relation to every second reappointment of a person after the person’s first appointment under subsection (1).

section.heading: Appointment of senior members and general members

content.p: Appointment by Governor-General
A senior member or general member is to be appointed by the Governor-General, by written instrument, on the recommendation of the Minister.
Before the Minister makes a recommendation to the Governor-General, the Minister must:
seek, and take into account, the advice of the President in relation to:
whether the appointment would meet the operational needs of the Tribunal; and
the financial capacity of the Tribunal for the appointment; and
the effect of the appointment on the number of senior members and general members relative to the number of Non-Judicial Deputy Presidents; and
be satisfied that the person was assessed, by a panel established under section 209, as suitable for the appointment through an assessment process that:
was merit-based; and
included public advertising of the position; and
complied with the requirements (if any) prescribed by the regulations.
Qualification for appointment—senior member
A person must not be appointed as a senior member unless:
the person is enrolled as a legal practitioner and has been so enrolled for at least 7 years; or
the Minister is satisfied that the person has at least 7 years’ specialised training or experience in a subject matter relevant to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.
Qualification for appointment—general member
A person must not be appointed as a general member unless:
the person is enrolled as a legal practitioner and has been so enrolled for at least 5 years; or
the Minister is satisfied that the person has at least 5 years’ specialised training or experience in a subject matter relevant to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.
Period of appointment
A senior member or general member holds office for a period of 5 years unless a shorter period is specified in the instrument of appointment.
If the instrument of appointment specifies a shorter period, the instrument must state the reasons why the shorter period is specified.
Basis of appointment
A senior member or general member may be appointed on a salaried or sessional basis.
Reappointment
A person may be reappointed as a senior member or general member by written instrument made within 6 months before the end of the period specified in the person’s instrument of appointment.

Before a person is reappointed as a senior member or general member, the Minister must seek, and take into account, the advice of the President in relation to the person’s performance against the performance standard.
Paragraph (2)(b) applies only in relation to every second reappointment of a person to an office after the person’s first appointment to that office under subsection (1).

(1) The Minister must, from time to time, establish one or more panels (assessment panels) of persons for the purposes of assessing whether a candidate or candidates are suitable for appointment under section 205, 207, 208 or 227.
The regulations may make provision for and in relation to assessment panels.
Without limiting subsection (2), the regulations may make provision for and in relation to the following:
the establishment of assessment panels;
the composition of assessment panels;
the operation and procedures of assessment panels;
the methodology to be used by assessment panels in assessing candidates for appointment as a member;
the provision of assistance by the Department to assessment panels, including secretariat services and clerical assistance.

section.heading: Appointment of a Judge not to affect tenure etc.

content.p: The appointment of a Judge as a member, or service by a Judge as a member, does not affect:
the Judge’s tenure of office as a Judge; or
the Judge’s rank, title, status, precedence, salary, annual or other allowances or other rights or privileges as the holder of the Judge’s office as a Judge.
For all purposes, the Judge’s service as a member is taken to be service as a Judge.
A member who is a Judge ceases to hold office as a member if the member ceases to be a Judge.

(1) The Minister may, at the request of the President and by written instrument, extend a member’s appointment if, apart from this section, the member’s appointment would cease to have effect (other than under section 220 or 221) on a day (the cessation day).
The extension must be made before the cessation day.
The extended appointment has effect until the earliest of the following:
the end of the period of 3 months after the cessation day;
if the member gives a resignation under section 220—the time when that resignation takes effect;
if the extended appointment is terminated under section 221—the time when that termination takes effect.
An instrument made under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.
President
The Minister may, by written instrument, appoint a person to act as the President:
during a vacancy in the office of President (whether or not an appointment has previously been made to the office); or
during any period, or during all periods, when the President:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the office.
Note: For rules that apply to acting appointments, see sections 33AB and 33A of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.
A person must not be appointed to act as the President in the circumstances mentioned in paragraph (1)(a) (vacancy in the office of President) unless:
the person is qualified, as mentioned in subsection 205(3), to be appointed as the President; and
the Minister has consulted the Chief Justice of the Federal Court.
(2A) A person must not be appointed to act as the President in the circumstances mentioned in paragraph (1)(b) (absence, etc.) unless:
either:
the person is qualified, as mentioned in subsection 205(3), to be appointed as the President; and
the Minister has consulted the Chief Justice of the Federal Court; or
the person is a member who is a Non-Judicial Deputy President.
An appointment of a member who is a Non-Judicial Deputy President to act as the President as mentioned in paragraph (2A)(b) must not be for a period of more than 3 weeks.
Other members
The Minister may, at the request of the President and by written instrument, appoint a person to act as a member other than the President:
during a vacancy in the office of a member other than the President (whether or not an appointment has previously been made to the office); or
during any period, or during all periods, when a member other than the President:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the office.
Note: For rules that apply to acting appointments, see sections 33AB and 33A of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.
A person must not be appointed to act as a member other than the President unless:
if the person is to act as a Judicial Deputy President:
the person is qualified, as mentioned in subsection 206(3), to be appointed as a Judicial Deputy President; and
the Minister has consulted the Chief Justice of the court of which the person is a Judge; or
if the person is to act as a Non-Judicial Deputy President—the person is qualified, as mentioned in subsection 207(3), to be appointed as a Non-Judicial Deputy President; or
if the person is to act as a senior member—the person is qualified, as mentioned in subsection 208(3), to be appointed as a senior member; or
if the person is to act as a general member—the person is qualified, as mentioned in subsection 208(4), to be appointed as a general member.
Extension of acting appointment

If a person has been appointed under this section to act as a member, the Minister may extend the person’s appointment if the Minister is satisfied that it is necessary to do so by reason of a pending proceeding or other special circumstances.
The extension must be made:
in writing; and
before the day that the member who was absent or unable to perform the duties of the member’s office returns to perform those duties.
The extension must not be for more than:
unless paragraph (b) applies—12 months; or
in the case of a Non-Judicial Deputy President appointed to act as the President as mentioned in paragraph (2A)(b)—3 weeks.
A person who is appointed or reappointed as a member or to act as a member must, before beginning to discharge the duties of the member’s office, take an oath or affirmation.

The oath or affirmation is an oath or affirmation that the person will well and truly serve in the office, and do right to all manner of people according to law without fear or favour, affection or ill-will.
An oath or affirmation to be taken by the President must be taken before:
the Governor-General; or
a Justice of the High Court; or
a Judge of the Federal Court; or
a Judge of the Supreme Court of a State or a Territory.
An oath or affirmation to be taken by a member other than the President must be taken before:
the Governor-General; or
a Justice of the High Court; or
a Judge of the Federal Court; or
a Judge of the Supreme Court of a State or a Territory; or
the President.
Subdivision B—Members’ terms and conditions

A non-judicial member is to be paid the remuneration that is determined by the Remuneration Tribunal. If no determination of that remuneration by the Remuneration Tribunal is in operation, the member is to be paid the remuneration that is prescribed by the rules.
A non-judicial member is to be paid the allowances that are prescribed by the rules.
(3) This section has effect subject to the Remuneration Tribunal Act 1973.
Salaried members
A salaried member has the recreation leave entitlements that are determined by the Remuneration Tribunal.
The Minister may grant the President leave of absence, other than recreation leave, on the terms and conditions as to remuneration or otherwise that the Minister determines.

The President may grant a salaried member (other than the President) leave of absence, other than recreation leave, on the terms and conditions as to remuneration or otherwise that the President determines.
Sessional members
The President may grant leave of absence to a sessional member on the terms and conditions that the President determines.
Salaried non-judicial members
A non-judicial member appointed on a salaried basis must not engage in paid work outside the duties of the member’s office without the President’s approval.
Sessional non-judicial members
A non-judicial member appointed on a sessional basis must not engage in any paid work that conflicts or could conflict with the proper performance of the member’s duties.
A person covered by subsection (2) must not appear in a proceeding in the Tribunal:
as a representative of a party to the proceeding; or
as an expert witness in the proceeding.
The following persons are covered by this subsection:
a member;
a person who ceased to be a member during:
the 12 months before the day of the appearance; or
if a law of a State or Territory has the effect of prescribing a longer period before the day of the appearance—that longer period.
Subsection (1) does not apply if the person has permission to appear in the proceeding from:
if the person is the President—the Minister; or
in any other case—the President.
General duty to disclose interests

If a member has an interest, pecuniary or otherwise, that conflicts or could conflict with the proper performance of the member’s duties, the member must disclose the nature of the interest to the President (or, if the member is the President, the Minister).
Disclosure of interests relating to proceedings
If a member who is:
a member of the Tribunal as constituted for the purposes of a proceeding; or
performing or exercising a function or power of the Tribunal in relation to a proceeding;
has an interest, pecuniary or otherwise, that conflicts or could conflict with the proper performance of the member’s duties in the proceeding, the member:
must disclose the nature of the interest to:
the parties to the proceeding; and
the President (or, if the member is the President, the Minister); and
must not take part in the proceeding or exercise any powers in relation to the proceeding unless the parties and the President (or, if the member is the President, the Minister) consent.
Timing of disclosure
A disclosure under this section must be made as soon as possible after the relevant facts have come to the member’s knowledge.
The President must keep a register of disclosures made under section 218.
The President may keep the register by electronic means.
The register must contain, for each disclosure:
the nature of the interest disclosed; and
any action taken as a result of the disclosure.
The register is not a legislative instrument.
A member may resign the member’s appointment by giving the Governor-General a written resignation.
The member must also give a copy of the written resignation to the President.
The resignation takes effect on the day it is received by the Governor-General or, if a later day is specified in the resignation, on that later day.
The Governor-General may, on the recommendation of the Minister, terminate the appointment of a non-judicial member if:
the member is convicted of an indictable offence; or
the member is unable to perform the duties of the member’s office because of physical or mental incapacity; or
the member’s conduct or behaviour amounts to serious misconduct by the member; or
the member is a salaried member and is absent, except on leave of absence, for 5 consecutive days or for 10 days in any 12 months; or
the member is a sessional member and is unavailable, except on leave of absence, to perform the duties of the member’s office for more than 3 months; or
the member engages in conduct that constitutes a serious breach of the code of conduct; or
the member engages in conduct that constitutes a serious breach of the performance standard; or
the member is a salaried member and engages, except with the President’s approval, in paid work outside the duties of the member’s office (see subsection 216(1)); or
the member is a sessional member and engages in paid work that conflicts or could conflict with the proper performance of the member’s duties (see subsection 216(2)); or
the member fails, without reasonable excuse, to comply with section 218 (disclosure of interests).
Without limiting the kinds of conduct that may constitute a serious breach of the code of conduct or performance standard for the purposes of paragraph (1)(f) or (g), such conduct includes:
repeatedly breaching the code of conduct or performance standard; and
breaching the code of conduct or performance standard in a way that is having, or is likely to have, a damaging effect on public trust and confidence in the Tribunal; and
breaching the code of conduct or performance standard and failing to comply with a direction under subsection 200(1) in relation to the breach.
The Governor-General must terminate the appointment of a non-judicial member if the member:
becomes bankrupt; or
applies to take the benefit of any law for the relief of bankrupt or insolvent debtors; or
compounds with the member’s creditors; or
makes an assignment of the member’s remuneration for the benefit of the member’s creditors.

section.heading: President must notify Minister about grounds for termination

content.p: If the President reasonably believes that there are grounds for terminating a non-judicial member’s appointment under section 221, the President must notify the Minister as soon as possible.
A non-judicial member holds office on the terms and conditions (if any) in relation to matters not covered by this Act that are determined by the Minister.
Subdivision A—Management functions of President

section.heading: Management of administrative affairs of Tribunal

content.p: The President is responsible for managing the administrative affairs of the Tribunal.
(2) The administrative affairs of the Tribunal do not include the corporate and registry services of the Tribunal.
Subdivision B—Appointment and functions of Principal Registrar
There is to be a Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar of the Administrative Review Tribunal.
The Principal Registrar has the following functions:
to assist the President in managing the administrative affairs of the Tribunal;
to assist the Tribunal to pursue the objective in section 9;
to provide the corporate and registry services of the Tribunal;
any other function conferred on the Principal Registrar by this Act or another Act;
to do anything incidental or conducive to the performance of any of the above functions.

Note: The Principal Registrar is also responsible for matters relating to the Tribunal under the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013 and the Public Service Act 1999 (see sections 238 and 241).
(2) The following matters relating to the Tribunal are the corporate and registry services of the Tribunal:
communications;
finance;
human resources;
the work health and safety of members, staff members and other persons interacting with the Tribunal;
information technology;
libraries;
records management;
administrative and case management support for proceedings in the Tribunal;
procurement and contract management;
property;
risk oversight and management;
security;
statistics;
any other matter prescribed by the rules.
The Principal Registrar is not subject to direction by the President in relation to the Principal Registrar’s performance or exercise of functions or powers under:
(a) the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013; or
(b) the Public Service Act 1999.
Appointment by Governor-General
The Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar is to be appointed by the Governor-General, by written instrument, on the recommendation of the Minister.
Before the Minister makes a recommendation to the Governor-General, the Minister must:
be satisfied that the person has appropriate qualifications, knowledge or experience; and
be satisfied that the person was assessed, by a panel established under section 209, as suitable for the appointment through an assessment process that:
was merit-based; and
included public advertising of the position; and
complied with the requirements (if any) prescribed by the regulations; and
obtain the agreement of the President to the appointment.
Period of appointment
The Principal Registrar holds office for a period of 5 years.
Basis of appointment
The Principal Registrar must be appointed on a salaried basis.
Reappointment

Paragraph (2)(b) does not apply in relation to the reappointment of a person who, immediately before the start of the period of reappointment, holds office as the Principal Registrar under a previous appointment under subsection (1).
The President may, by written instrument, appoint a person to act as the Principal Registrar:
during a vacancy in the office of Principal Registrar (whether or not an appointment has previously been made to the office); or
during any period, or during all periods, when the Principal Registrar:
is absent from duty or from Australia; or
is, for any reason, unable to perform the duties of the office.
Note: For rules that apply to acting appointments, see sections 33AB and 33A of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.

The Principal Registrar is to be paid the remuneration that is determined by the Remuneration Tribunal. If no determination of that remuneration by the Remuneration Tribunal is in operation, the Principal Registrar is to be paid the remuneration that is prescribed by the rules.
The Principal Registrar is to be paid the allowances that are prescribed by the rules.
(3) This section has effect subject to the Remuneration Tribunal Act 1973.
The Principal Registrar has the recreation leave entitlements that are determined by the Remuneration Tribunal.
The President may grant the Principal Registrar leave of absence, other than recreation leave, on the terms and conditions as to remuneration or otherwise that the Minister determines.
The Principal Registrar must not engage in paid work outside the duties of the Principal Registrar’s office without the President’s approval.

(1) A disclosure by the Principal Registrar under section 29 of the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013 (which deals with the duty to disclose interests) must be made to the President.
Subsection (1) applies in addition to any rules made for the purposes of that section.
